paras: The lynching of Henry Tanner, John Tanner and Alonzo Smith was the hanging of three Black prisoners by a masked crowd that took them from the jail at Oxford, Granville County, North Carolina, at about 2 a.m. on Sunday, September 2, 1888. The Tanners, father and son, were charged with murdering an elderly Black man, Squire Grissom, and Smith with arson or burglary and arson. A Raleigh dispatch called it a lynching "such as was never before recorded in the history of the State."

According to the Richmond Dispatch, Grissom was killed in his Brassfield township cabin on June 16, 1888, and found days later; the Raleigh wire dated the finding to June 21 and said his head had been cut off. Henry Tanner, his son John, Lucy Cannady and Grissom's daughter Dora were arrested on suspicion, and the Dispatch's Oxford correspondent wrote that Dora had since confessed she saw the Tanners kill her father. Smith was awaiting trial for breaking into and burning the house of James Thomasson.

After threats of lynching, the sheriff asked the Governor for troops and the Granville Grays guarded the jail for several nights. Their commander, Capt. W. A. Bobbitt, wrote that they were told on the 27th of August that their services were no longer needed.

Early on Sunday a party of men rode in from the country, about fifty according to the Oxford special and seventy-five to a hundred according to the Raleigh wire. They broke into the sheriff's office for the jail keys, overpowered the lone guard, seized a policeman and took the two Tanners and Smith from the steel cells, leaving the other prisoners. The three were hanged on one tree at the edge of town, Tanner and his son on the same limb, and died by strangulation. The policeman rang the militia alarm, but the troops arrived too late, and the bodies were buried that afternoon.

A coroner's jury reached no decision and adjourned until September 6 to seek the lynchers' identity; no report of its finding or of any arrest appears in the coverage. The Western Sentinel noted that thirteen more prisoners awaited trial for their lives and that threats had been made against a white couple named Adcock. A Raleigh letter later counted Oxford as one of two triple lynchings among thirteen in the state that year.

The Richmond Dispatch printed the Oxford telegram under "Fearful Vengeance" with its correspondent's account and a history of the crime. The Raleigh wire reached Washington, Indianapolis, New York and Maine on September 4 as "A Triple Lynching" or "Three Negroes Lynched." Weekly digests in Kentucky, Kansas and Dakota cut it to a line, some placing it at "Raleigh, S. C." or dating it the 3d, and one called the victims "three negro criminals."

North Carolina papers deplored the lynching but blamed the courts. The Henderson Gold Leaf held that "the law itself, or the ministers of the law, are responsible for it," saying the Tanners, "if guilty," deserved their fate but Smith did not. The Western Sentinel traced Granville's "repeated lynching" to tardy justice and jail breaking. The Dispatch's correspondent called the lynching "deeply regretted by all law-abiding citizens," while a Raleigh dispatch in the Maysville Evening Bulletin called the dead criminals "hated by both whites and blacks" and the evidence against the untried Tanners "very positive."

Most reports give about 2 a.m. on September 2, but the Sun gave about 3 o'clock and some later items the 3d. Crowd estimates ran from about fifty to about a hundred, and one reprint named the younger Tanner "Jim."

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Tanner, John Tanner and Alonzo Smith
bases: A masked crowd took three Black prisoners from the Oxford jail and hanged them (A2, A7, A18).

Three jailed men were hanged by a masked crowd estimated at fifty to a hundred, without lawful authority, after the jail guard was overpowered (A2, A7, A16); the victims were awaiting trial on murder and arson charges, so the killing was carried out as punishment for alleged crimes (A6, A18).

Separate accounts from Oxford (Dispatch/News and Observer special), the Raleigh wire, a longer Raleigh dispatch and the Granville Grays commander's letter agree on the three names, the jail seizure and the hanging (A2, A3, A7, A16, A18, A30).

accounts.label: Oxford special (Dispatch / News and Observer)
accounts.gist: About fifty men took the three from jail about 2 a.m. and hanged them on one tree; the Grays had recently been taken off guard and the military came too late.

accounts.label: Dispatch Oxford correspondent
accounts.gist: Sixty to a hundred men from a distant part of the county, Black and white, broke into the sheriff's office for the keys and hanged the three to a post-oak at the edge of town.

accounts.label: Raleigh wire
accounts.gist: Seventy-five to a hundred masked men, white and Black, overpowered the lone guard, took the keys from the sheriff's drawer and hanged the three; the coroner's jury adjourned without a decision.

accounts.label: Longer Raleigh dispatch
accounts.gist: About a hundred mounted, disguised men picketed the approaches, seized the jailer and a policeman, and rode off with the prisoners; it asserted the Tanners' guilt was 'very positive'.

accounts.label: Granville Grays commander
accounts.gist: Capt. Bobbitt wrote that a crowd of whites and Blacks from the country did the work quickly, and that the Grays had been told on the 27th their services were no longer needed.

framing.detail: The Gold Leaf ('Judge Lynch Holds High Car nival') called the affair horrible but blamed 'the laxity of the law' and said Smith's offense did not deserve such judgment.
The Western Sentinel attributed Granville's repeated lynchings to 'tardy justice' and jail breaking.
The Dispatch's Oxford correspondent said the lynching was 'deeply regretted by all law-abiding citizens'.
The Evening Bulletin's Raleigh dispatch called the victims 'three criminals who were hated by both whites and blacks' and called the evidence 'very positive'.
Northern and western papers ran the Raleigh wire under headlines like 'Three Negroes Lynched' or as one-line digest items.
